analysis.one_liner: Lets pharmacies and individuals legally import cheaper prescription drugs from Canada.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and died there with no hearing, no vote, and no action for the rest of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal drug law so wholesalers, pharmacies, and individuals can import qualifying prescription drugs from Canada without the special HHS approval the law currently requires, and later from other advanced countries. It extends eligibility to insulin, dialysis solutions, and biological drugs, lets people fill U.S. prescriptions through certified foreign pharmacies for up to a 90-day supply, and adds safety rules: certified sellers, product testing, import tracing, criminal penalties for counterfeit-drug websites, and bans on manufacturers blocking or overcharging foreign sellers. It was introduced in March 2021 and referred to committee, where it stalled.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. prices for prescription drugs, especially people on expensive brand-name drugs, insulin, and biologics. U.S. pharmacies and wholesalers could import lower-priced versions, and individuals could order a 90-day personal supply from certified Canadian pharmacies using their U.S. prescription.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People paying high U.S. drug prices

how_it_helps.text: Removes the current requirement that HHS certify to Congress before allowing drug importation from Canada, instead ordering HHS to write regulations permitting importation of qualifying drugs [S2].

Expands eligible drugs beyond the current law to include insulin, peritoneal dialysis solution, and biological products, categories that include some of the most expensive medicines Americans buy [S2] [S3].
Lets individuals fill a U.S.-issued prescription through a certified licensed foreign pharmacy for personal use in up to a 90-day supply, instead of needing an HHS waiver [S2].
Adds anti-circumvention rules: drug makers may not charge foreign sellers more than other buyers in the same country, cut off their supply, or alter the product to defeat importation [S3].

Imposes safety machinery: certified foreign sellers with at least five years of operation, Secretary-approved laboratory testing, import tracing, suspension authority for counterfeit or recalled drugs, and up to 10 years' imprisonment or a $250,000 fine for websites selling counterfeit drugs or dispensing without a valid prescription [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which currently sustain higher U.S. prices partly because reimportation from lower-priced countries is barred. They would also bear the cost of compliance with the anti-discrimination and supply rules.

drawbacks.text: Safety risk is the standard objection to drug importation: once drugs cross borders, chain-of-custody is harder to police, and counterfeit or substandard products can slip in; the bill answers this with certification, testing, and tracing requirements, but those systems are only as good as their enforcement [S3].

Canada's drug market is small relative to the United States, so large-scale U.S. importation could strain Canada's supply and cause shortages there; the bill's answer is to first require evidence of U.S. consumer savings before expanding beyond Canada, but it does not cap volumes [S3].
The bill relies on HHS to write and enforce detailed regulations within 180 days of enactment, so its real-world effect would depend heavily on how a given administration implemented it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households buying expensive brand-name drugs, the potential savings are substantial, and the bill is unusually detailed about safety for an importation bill — certification, lab testing, tracing, and criminal penalties for counterfeit sellers are all built in. The honest caveats are real but manageable: enforcement quality determines whether imported drugs are as safe as domestic ones, and Canada's capacity to supply the U.S. market is limited. The bill's biggest weakness is not design but fate — it never got any committee consideration at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, sent to its Health Subcommittee the next day, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 23, 2021, by Rep. Peter Welch with eight original cosponsors, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
On March 24, 2021, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill gathered 16 cosponsors, all Democrats, but never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote in the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose U.S. pricing is preserved so long as cheaper foreign supplies stay barred; American patients kept paying U.S. prices for insulin, biologics, and other qualifying drugs.

for.name: Rep. Peter Welch
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled eight original cosponsors on introduction day.

for.name: 16 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro and progressive members (Bush, Doggett, Norton, Pocan, Khanna, Neguse, Omar, Schakowsky)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; the bill died in committee with no action after its subcommittee referral.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Manufacturers of patented and brand-name drugs
against.what_they_did: Long opposed drug importation legislation, arguing it threatens the drug supply and undercuts U.S. prices; importation bills have repeatedly died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists, but support was entirely from one party.

industries.note: Their business model relies on charging higher prices in the U.S. than abroad, which importation from Canada would erode. The bill explicitly outlaws overcharging or cutting off foreign sellers to block importation, striking at the supply controls that keep U.S. prices high [S3].

industries.industry: Licensed Canadian pharmacies and foreign wholesale distributors
industries.note: They would become the certified channel for cheaper drugs to U.S. patients, earning fees and new customers. Their interest runs with patients' interest in lower prices [S3].

industries.industry: U.S. pharmacies and wholesale drug distributors
industries.note: They could import qualifying drugs at lower cost and pass some savings on, gaining a purchasing option; but cheaper foreign channels, including online foreign pharmacies serving individuals directly, would also compete with them [S2] [S3].
